title: Query evaluation: processing models
lead: Iterator interfaces, operator state, pipelining, vectorisation and materialisation.

sections.title: Iterator interface and control flow
sections.html:
A processing model defines how operators execute a physical plan and pass results between them. In the iterator model, each operator implements open(), next() and close(), maintaining its own execution state.

The query processor opens the root and repeatedly requests its next tuple until EOF, then closes it. Operators call their children through the same interface. Control is pulled from the root towards the leaves; tuples return towards the root.

The interface allows arbitrary operator composition. A parent need not know whether its child is a scan, filter or join. LIMIT can stop requesting further tuples once enough results have been produced, subject to work already required by blocking operators.

PDF pp. 1–5

sections.title: Stateful operator implementations
sections.html:
A selection’s next() repeatedly asks its child for a tuple until a predicate succeeds or EOF is reached. A heap scan tracks the current page and slot so that the next call resumes from the correct position.

A nested-loop join also remembers the current outer tuple and its position in the inner scan. After exhausting the inner input, it resets that input and advances the outer tuple. Returning one match must preserve state for the following call.

The two-pass sort example blocks during initial run generation, then its next() performs the final merge. The source assumes enough buffers to merge the generated runs in one final pass. More runs require additional merge passes.

PDF pp. 6–11

sections.title: Pipelining and vectorisation
sections.html:
Pipelining passes tuples through successive operators without first writing the entire intermediate relation. It can reduce temporary storage and time to the first output. A sort must consume input before returning globally sorted output; a hash join must build its hash table before probing.

Tuple-at-a-time iterators incur a function call for each tuple at each operator and maintain resume state. This overhead can limit CPU efficiency even when I/O is small.

The vectorised model returns batches instead of individual tuples. It amortises calls and bookkeeping across several tuples and enables tight loops and SIMD processing. Batching changes the execution interface, not relational query semantics.

PDF pp. 12–15

sections.title: Materialisation model
sections.html:
In the materialisation model, an operator consumes its input and produces its entire output before the parent proceeds. Evaluation moves bottom-up through the plan.

Processing complete collections can improve code and data locality, especially when intermediate results are small. Large analytical intermediates instead increase memory use and may spill to disk. “Materialisation” therefore describes a transfer boundary; whether the result resides in memory or on disk depends on its size and implementation.

The source contrasts tuple-at-a-time iterators, batch-at-a-time vectorisation and result-at-a-time materialisation. Operator blocking requirements remain relevant in each model.

PDF pp. 16–18

quiz.question: Can one Filter.next() call invoke child.next() more than once?
options: Yes, to discard tuples that do not satisfy the predicate
No, it always calls the child exactly once
Only when the child is an index
quiz.explanation: The filter continues reading input until it finds a qualifying tuple or reaches EOF.

source.summary: The full official PDF has been reviewed. Coverage includes the open/next/close iterator interface and composability; selection, heap-scan, and nested-loop state; blocking sorts and hash builds; pipelining, LIMIT, and iterator overhead; vectorized batch and SIMD processing; and materialization, execution direction, and workload trade-offs. The explanations and calculations are original teaching material rather than reproductions of the slides.
